newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Opposition activists hide from Phnom Penh police.
newsitem.headline: Opposition activists hide from Phnom Penh police.

text.p: Down a dark, muddy alley, past rusted metal gates and lines of laundry hanging limp in the night is a small "safe house" where five Cambodian opposition political activists have holed up to avoid arrest.
Relatives keep watch on the alley while the five men lounge in a small, dimly-lit room rank with the smell of sweat.
A tiny wall fan whirs over the noise of the television, moving fetid air across their anxious faces.

The five activists have been on the run since the weekend of July 5-6, when Phnom Penh erupted in violence as troops loyal to Second Prime Minister Hun Sen overthrew Cambodia's First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, These are not big name politicians, nor men who would command the interest of a Western embassy and possible asylum.
They are small fish left gasping in the rapidly shrinking pond of Cambodian democracy.
"Of course we are afraid. People are being arrested and some have been killed," said one of the men, a youth leader in Prince Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC Party.
Ranging in age from 22 to 31, representing both FUNCINPEC and the Khmer Nation Party (KNP), which is allied with FUNCINPEC, the activists have no money or connections to flee.
They cling to obscure bits of paper and identity cards proving their former party positions -- hoping one or the other credential will prove a passport to freedom.
The men are uncertain if their lives are actively at risk and Western rights workers with whom they have consulted have no clear idea either.
But with Western officials reporting that up to 40 people have died in government custody since the coup, none of the five is willing to find out whether he is a target.
Many opposition activists like them are in hiding across Cambodia and others have fled the country.
All have concluded that even if their lives are not at risk their ability to study or work in Cambodia is at an end so long as Hun Sen remains the source of all power.
"All we are asking for is help getting out of the country. So long as we remain in Phnom Penh we can do nothing," said one of the FUNCINPEC activists, an earnest young man of 22.
"I want the United Nations to come to Cambodia again to solve this problem. We cannot resolve this ourselves. Hun Sen is using violence to try to ban FUNCINPEC and KNP supporters."
As if to prove the point the men play a video of a grenade attack on a KNP rally in Phnom Penh in March in which up to 19 persons were killed.

Gruesome footage of the attack, which many now reckon was the first incident in Cambodia's current cycle of political violence, shows gravely wounded civilians lying unattended on the blood-soaked ground.
The Washington Post reported the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation implicated Hun Sen's faction in the attack.

In a country still shuddering from years of war under the Lon Nol regime in the early 1970's, and from the genocidal madness of Pol Pot and the Khmer Rouge later that decade, the recent violence in Phnom Penh awakens old fears.

Only one of the five activists at the safe house, Keo (not his real name), 31, actually remembers Pol Pot's time. Keo's journey, and that of his family, mirror Cambodia's turbulent history over the past four decades.
His father, a high official in the pre-Lon Nol government, once lived with his mother in the Royal palace.
Then, as a soldier under the Lon Nol regime, his father fought the Khmer Rouge and disappeared near the end of the war, allegedly while on a last-ditch mission with U.S. troops.
Keo and his mother went to the countryside under the Khmer Rouge. "We were slaves like everybody else," he said.
More than one million Cambodians died during the Khmer Rouge's 1975-79 "killing fields" regime.

Returning to Phnom Penh in 1979 after the Khmer Rouge were driven out by a Vietnamese invasion force, Keo took up his studies, went into the army and finally, in 1994, became a youth leader under Prince Ranariddh.

"I don't think about money or rank, but because my father was once a government official I want to continue his work in politics," Keo said in a voice so soft it could hardly be heard over the sound of the fan.
A barking dog and the slam of a gate bring the conversation to a sudden halt. Lights are doused and reporters shown the door as the five young men slip off quietly into the night.
